support_summary: D1: questions were all clinician evidence requests in the in-house database since 2010 meeting stated eligibility, excluding post-April 2023 requests (Methods); D2: standardised COSTAR prompt printed in Figure 1 and run dates 25 March-1 April 2024 on internal aiChat GPT-4 are stated, but no exact GPT-4 release string; D3: no temperature or other generation settings are reported, only the decision to submit each question once after a 5-question x 5-run variability test; D4: references were searched on PubMed, Google, Google Scholar and journal websites and documented found/not found; D5/D6: the citation subset was assigned to librarian pairs who 'independently attempted to locate all cited references', but the same librarian team also submitted the questions and no agreement figure or disagreement rule for citation verification is reported; D7: no rule for near matches is stated - references were simply found or not found, so partial matches are folded silently into the 60/162 verified count; D8: the 30% citation subset (66 questions, 162 references) was randomly selected with a random number generator and all results for the single arm are reported.

D1: 21 questions were designed by two researchers (K.Z. and S.J.S.) on only two common diseases (hypertension, diabetes) and two rare diseases (ALS, laryngeal cancer), US only and pre-2021, with the list in Table S1; D2: questions in Table S1 and data collection 31 October-17 November 2023 are stated, but ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4 and Bard carry no exact version strings; D3: a new session per question and two submissions on different dates are stated, but no settings (temperature, browsing state) are reported; D4: authenticity was judged by 'internet search' with no named bibliographic source, although categories covered wrong authors, journal, volume, pages, DOI and hyperlinks (Table 1 footnotes); D5/D6: the paper never states who evaluated reference relevance/authenticity or whether that check was duplicated or blinded - a single researcher (K.Z.) input all questions and the benchmark search was verified by S.J.S. only; D7: authentic, incomplete, inaccurate and fabricated are defined in Methods and counted apart (Bard unique references: 44 authentic, 5 incomplete, 7 inaccurate, 9 fabricated; Table 1); D8: all three models and all 21 questions are reported, including ChatGPT-3.5 providing no references and the exploratory benchmark-feeding analysis (Table S10).

D1: the 201 cases were taken sequentially as published from NEJM (plus 36 Friedman cases) with varied demographics and specialties (Introduction; Appendix S1), a stated sequential frame; D2: sample prompts are in Appendices S2-S4 and the model is named ChatGPT-4, but no generation date and no exact version string are stated; D3: no generation settings are reported at all, and it is not stated which of the five sequential runs supplied the verified citations; D4: 'the authors conducted an internet search for each correct diagnosis to confirm the reference citation' - no database is named, though citations and DOIs are scored separately (34.8% and 37.8%); D5: the authors who designed and ran the prompts also did the citation search, with no separation stated; D6: the paper never states how many people verified citations, whether it was duplicated or blinded, or any agreement figure; D7: correct, incorrect and non-existent are counted apart (70, 91 and 40 citations; 76, 83 and 42 DOIs) but the rule distinguishing incorrect from non-existent appears only beside the results, not as a pre-stated methods definition; D8: all panel sizes (2-10 plus model-chosen) and all four research questions are reported with counts.

D1: a single condition, Peyronie's disease, with 9 NIH frequently asked questions plus 11 NIH presurgical questions - a published question set but one narrow topic; D2: models and engines are named (ChatGPT GPT-3.5, Bard PaLM2, Bing AI GPT-4 in 'balanced' mode, DocsGPT GPT-4) and rounds ran October 2023 and April 2024, but no exact version strings and the optimising prompt is shown only in Figure 1; D3: private browser, conversation deleted before each query and prompted/unprompted arms are stated, but no other settings are reported; D4: citation validity was checked by following the cited source/hyperlink - no bibliographic database (PubMed, Crossref or similar) is named as the verification source; D5/D6: 'each time that an LLM cited a source, 2 reviewers (J.C., S.Y.W.) verified its validity', separate from the three DISCERN reviewers, but blinding of the citation verifiers and any agreement figure are not reported; D7: four scenarios (confirmed source/contains information, confirmed/hallucinated information, hallucinated source/contains information, hallucinated/hallucinated) are defined in Methods and counted apart (108, 28, 16 and 101 of 254); D8: all four LLMs are reported and Bard's three refused questions are disclosed, but citation counts are given only for the prompted cohort (Appendix A2).

D1: a single, deliberately stable topic (acne vulgaris, chosen so management 'has not changed significantly') with a 23-item questionnaire developed by one experienced dermatologist (L.N.) from forum questions and textbooks; D2: ChatGPT version 4, study dates 19-21 September 2023, no plugins/internet browsing and English language are stated, but no exact release string and the full prompt wording is only in the supplementary tables; D3: three independent operators prompted each question three times in separate sessions and first-session references were the ones verified, but no temperature or other settings are reported; D4: quotation correctness (authors, title, journal, year, issue, pages) was checked against PubMed alone, with no second source before a reference was called a hallucination; D5: the paper never states who performed the PubMed hallucination check - the five-dermatologist panel scored references only after hallucinations were excluded; D6: the panel scored references independently with Gwet AC1 0.67 for pertinence/relevance/update, but duplicate verification of existence itself is not stated; D7: 17 'AI hallucinations' (any field error or combination) are counted in Supplementary Table 4, folding real papers with wrong fields in with invented ones, and it is unclear whether the 69 rated references include or exclude them; D8: all 23 questions and all three sessions are reported, with reference rating limited to the first session as stated in Methods.

D1: the authors designed 10 common uveitis cases, all listed in full (HLA-B27, birdshot, VKH, ARN, JIA and others), with the same five management questions per case - author-chosen with the list printed; D2: the prompt is printed verbatim ('Please answer the following questions in a highly specialized medical language as if you were an expert in uveitis...') and the paid ChatGPT '4.o (2024)' is named, but no exact version string or run dates are given; D3: each question was presented three times in separate sessions and all three attempts were analysed, but no settings or retry rule are reported; D4: references were checked across PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar; D5: author contributions show I.S. created the questions and interrogated the LLM and I.S./J.R. reviewed and classified the answers, so generation and verification overlap in the same two authors; D6: references 'were independently verified' and two uveitis specialists graded answers independently with discussion of disagreements, but the reported kappas measure agreement between attempts, not between reference verifiers, and no verifier agreement for citations is given; D7: accurate/correctly cited (22/52), not located in any database (22/52) and existing but misinterpreted or incorrectly cited (8/52) are counted apart, but the category definitions appear with the results rather than as a pre-stated rule; D8: all 10 cases, five questions and three attempts are tabulated (Table 1) for the single model.

D1: 30 questions on a single topic (COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction) developed by fellowship-trained rhinologists 'based on the most common patient inquiries seen in practice', in four stated categories; D2: the three prompting texts are printed verbatim in Table 1 and the model is given as ChatGPT (February 3, 2024, version) on GPT-4 via the publicly available website, but the 30 question wordings are not printed; D3: memory was reset before each prompting style, questions were posed in identical order within one thread per style and each prompt entered once, but no other settings are reported; D4: a reference counted as real if it 'has a DOI and is findable online' - no named bibliographic database and no check of authors, journal, year or pages; D5/D6: the paper never states who investigated the references or whether that verification was duplicated or blinded - the four rhinologists are described only as scoring answer quality (GQS); D7: only a real/falsified binary is reported for the 12 unique references (11 legitimate, 1 falsified), with no rule or separate count for partially matching references, and denominators shift between 27 total, 24 and 12 unique references in the text; D8: all four prompt arms are reported for quality scores, but reference results are not broken down by arm beyond stating all unique references came from the references prompt.

D1: 16 imaginary oral-pathology scenarios prepared by the authors, deliberately stripped of characteristic features and not histopathologically confirmed - a small author-created set; D2: the prompt format is printed verbatim ('List the three most likely diagnoses... and support them with citations from the literature'), models are named exactly as DeepSeek-V3 and ChatGPT-4o, all questions were asked on 18 February 2025 and the free versions were used; D3: search history and cookies were deleted before each question and each model was asked once (repeatability explicitly not assessed), but no settings or browsing state are reported; D4: references were searched in Google Scholar, PubMed and Web of Science and labelled 'real' if found there and 'fake' if not, with no field-by-field or DOI check described; D5/D6: the paper never states who searched the references or whether that check was duplicated - the blinding described covers only the 20 specialists scoring diagnoses, not citation verification; D7: no partial-match rule exists - a binary real/fake label folds real papers with wrong bibliographic fields into 'real' if findable and gives no partial counts apart (repetitions are noted in Table 2 only); D8: all 16 scenarios and both models are reported, with reference counts per model (DeepSeek-V3 48, 8 fake; ChatGPT-4o 62, 50 fake; Table 2).

D1: a single surgical topic, penile prosthesis implantation, chosen as technically detailed and well documented, with prompts developed by a single author (Limitations); D2: the complete prompt list is in Supplementary File 1 and the opening prompt is printed verbatim, and the interface is stated to be the publicly available web-based ChatGPT, but there is no generation date and, as the authors note, no 'fixed API version or model snapshot' for ChatGPT-5; D3: the authors state 'No iterative refinement or performance-based prompt selection was performed' and only the first complete output per prompt was evaluated, with exactly five references per section predefined, but no settings are reported; D4: references were 'independently verified using PubMed, Google Scholar, CrossRef, and, when necessary, the official journal websites' with title, authorship, journal, year, volume/issue, pages and DOI cross-checked; D5: one of the two verifiers (F.O.) also conceived the study and acquired/generated the data, so verification overlaps generation for that reviewer; D6: all classifications were performed independently by two reviewers (M.G., F.O.) with discrepancies resolved by consensus after re-verification, but the reported ICCs (0.95, 0.97) are for the SANRA/rubric quality scores, not for citation classification agreement; D7: three predefined categories (fully accurate; partially inaccurate - real publication with one or more wrong elements, minor errors not fabrication; fabricated - no corresponding publication in major databases) are counted apart (35.7% fully accurate, about 17.9% fabricated, remainder partial); D8: all sections are reported, but five references per section across a seven-section outline does not reconcile with the reported total of 28 citations and the gap is not explained in the main text.

D1: a single topic, fertility preservation in men and prepubertal boys, chosen because adult FP is well documented and prepubertal FP is evolving, and the authors are FP experts; D2: all prompts are detailed in Supplementary Information with several printed verbatim, and the model is ChatGPT-4, but no generation date or exact version string and no interface are stated; D3: the outline prompt was re-run after the first outline omitted spermatogenesis and section prompts were then built from the model's own outline; for reproducibility the model 'was prompted a second time with the same prompt... and the first answer was the one included', but no settings are reported; D4: provided references 'were authenticated in PubMed or Google Scholar by the authors' and, where given, title, journal, authors and DOI were all verified; D5: both authors (M.S., K.E.O.) verified references and M.S. also wrote all the prompts and created the manuscript, so one verifier generated the material; D6: the two experts independently scored relevance, depth and currentness, but duplicate or blinded verification of reference authenticity itself is not stated and no agreement figure for it is given; D7: accurate (9/25), correct title but other fictitious parameters (12/25) and completely fictitious (4/25) are defined by full-parameter checking and counted apart; D8: all five reference sections (25 references, five per section) and all statements requiring citation (27, four inaccurate) are reported for the single model.

D1: a single, very recent topic (COVID-19 and musculoskeletal health, one of three topics in the wider project) where most literature post-dates the model's September 2021 cutoff, a choice that leans toward sparse/recent material; D2: the complete query lists are in Supplementary Materials 1 and 2, and the model is named ChatGPT 4.0, but no exact version string and no dates of querying are stated, and the AI-assisted arm used the AskYourPDF plugin; D3: the arms ran under different, stated conditions - AI-only from queries alone, AI-assisted given the human outline and human-selected references with a limit of 8-10 articles per subsection, queries kept in one chat with like/dislike feedback that the authors say improved results - and no settings are reported; D4: references were fact-checked by the co-authors with error fields enumerated (authors, journal, title, year, volume/issue, pages, DOIs), but no bibliographic source or database used for the checking is named; D5: 'all review articles were extensively fact-checked and edited by all co-authors', the same team that wrote the queries and generated the drafts; D6: checking by all co-authors is stated, but no independent duplicate process, blinding or agreement figure for citation checking is reported; D7: AI-only references are counted apart as non-existent (19/113), existing but incorrect in a named field (31/113) and misattributed (30/113), whereas the AI-assisted arm's 18/89 'incorrect' folds misattribution and plagiarism together without a split; D8: the abandoned AI-only arm is disclosed with its reason (cutoff overlap with AI-assisted) and its reference counts are still reported in Table 3, and the other two project topics are pointed to companion papers.

D1: 78 pharmacology items from the Korean Comprehensive Basic Medical Sciences Examination 2019-2021 form a stated exam frame, but 27 figure items were excluded and the taxonomy mix is recall-heavy (56.4% recall, 17.9% problem-solving, as the author notes); D2: all four lead-in prompts are printed word for word, the run is dated to ChatGPT 'versions between Jan/28/2023 and Jan/29/2023' powered by GPT-3.5, and chat history handling is described; D3: one question was fed at a time with previous chat history deleted before each submission and every output evaluated, but no settings are reported; D4: reference URLs were followed and authors searched on PubMed, Amazon and Google and titles on PubMed - matching the fields the prompts requested (URL, title, authors); D5: a single author (W.C.) 'designed and performed the current study including the translation', prompting and evaluation, so verifier and generator are the same person with no separation; D6: that single, unblinded author made judgement-based binary correctness calls on all references with no second verifier and no agreement check; D7: no whole-reference partial-match rule is stated - errors are counted apart by component (URLs wrong/nonexistent 191/274, authors not found 59/350, titles incorrect 148/152, Table 4), while the headline 69.7% 'incorrect citations' rests on the URL criterion alone; D8: all four prompts and 78 items are reported, but the additional textbook-only prompt modification is reported only as 'data not shown'.

D1: 20 questions on a single topic (oral cancer) selected from Google Trends (filters and 16 October 2023 search date stated) and clinic patient questions - the authors themselves note the selection 'lack[s] standardization'; D2: the model is ChatGPT-3.5 (released 30 November 2022), questions were entered on 16 October 2023 and the question list is in Supplemental 1, but no prompt asking for references is described and no exact version string is given; D3: a new registration was created and search history and cookies cleared before the session, with one output per question, but no other settings are reported; D4: 'References were searched manually in the Microsoft Edge browser and verified. References with a "page not found" error or links to advertising pages were considered fake' - a single browser search with no named bibliographic database settles existence, and broken links count as fabrication; D5: 'All phases of the research were performed by M.C.', so the person who ran the questions also verified the references; D6: that verification was single and unblinded with no duplicate check - the reported Fleiss/Cohen kappas cover the specialists' answer scores, not reference verification; D7: references are reported only as 13 scientific articles, 10 fake and the remainder website data, with no rule or separate count for real articles with wrong fields; D8: all 20 questions and all 81 references are accounted for in the reported categories for the single model.

D1: two topics were deliberately balanced across both models - ankle osteoarthritis chosen as broad and intra-articular calcaneal fractures as a niche subspecialty topic - with identical prompts to each model; D2: all prompts are listed in Appendix Figures 1A and 2A and the arms are named (ChatGPT-4 with the ScholarAI plugin; Assistant by scite), but no exact version strings and no generation dates are stated; D3: prompts were identical across arms, generated text and references were copied unchanged, and the plugin difference between arms is stated, but no settings and no retry/selection rule are reported; D4: citation veracity was verified 'by referencing previously peer-reviewed literature and UpToDate', which settles existence and content support but not bibliographic field accuracy, and no database or DOI check is named; D5: the study authors who wrote the prompts and collected the data (J.W., N.N.) also graded the citations, mitigated by initial blinding to authorship; D6: authors were 'initially blinded to the authorship of the paper and individually graded each sentence and citation as either true or false', with discrepancies discussed to consensus - duplicate blinded verification, though no agreement figure is reported; D7: a citation was accurate only if it referenced a published paper AND contained the cited information, so misattributed real papers and missing citations are folded into the single inaccurate percentage, with missing-citation counts given in Table 2 (4, 8, 26 and 12) but no fabricated count apart; D8: all four AI papers (two models x two topics) and both human papers are reported with citation accuracies.

D1: a single, well-established topic - the ABCDE trauma protocol, chosen because of 'the vast resources available on the subject' - leans to settled, heavily referenced material where accurate references are easiest to produce; D2: the reference prompt is printed verbatim ('Please provide PubMed-indexed references to support each of the 5 steps mentioned above'), the model is ChatGPT version 4.0 (ChatGPT Plus) at chat.openai.com and the date is exact (27 November 2023); D3: prompting continued until six references per category were obtained (30 total) and no settings are reported, including the browsing state the authors note ChatGPT-4 had gained in September 2023; D4: a reference was 'nonexistent' only if title, authors, journal and year did not match and it could not be found on PubMed, Google Scholar, Cochrane, Embase or Scopus, with all field discrepancies against PubMed reviewed and bolded (Table III); D5: the two reviewers are study team members and the paper does not state that they were separate from the investigator who posed the questions; D6: 'Two independent reviewers... classified the 30 references' on the 0-2 scale with Cohen's kappa 0.89 reported and both scores averaged by a stated rule; D7: the grading system is defined in Methods/Table II before results (0 nonexistent, 1 inaccurate - wrong or missing author, year, title, volume, pages or PMID, 2 accurate) and counts are given apart (13 accurate, 13 inaccurate, 4 nonexistent); D8: all five ABCDE categories and all 30 references are reported.

D1: 17 TKA and 16 THA preoperative questions formulated by fellowship-trained surgeons 'based on common questions posed by patients in the clinical setting' - author-chosen, with full transcripts in Supporting Files 1 and 2; D2: the model is the open-access ChatGPT-3.5, questions were posed on 2 November 2023 and the first question's peer-reviewed-literature wording is printed, but there is no exact version string and later questions rely on the conversation carry-over rather than printed prompts; D3: TKA and THA were asked in separate, otherwise blank conversations in a single run, with the peer-reviewed instruction given only in the first question because ChatGPT 'will adjust its methods... for all subsequent questions', and no settings are reported; D4: each source 'was queried on PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, and Google Scholar' and was accurate only if authors, title, journal, year and DOI all matched - multiple sources covering every field; D5: source verification is described in the passive voice and response validity was appraised by the same authors who formulated and posed the questions; D6: the paper never states that source verification was duplicated or blinded, and for response appraisal 'Discrepancies among evaluators were not addressed'; D7: the all-fields-must-match rule is stated in Methods, but partial matches are folded into the single inaccurate count (70/109) with no split between fabricated and real-but-wrong-field references; D8: all 33 questions and 109 sources are reported per procedure, with duplicates among accurate sources disclosed (39 accurate, 32 unique).

D1: 12 nephrology topics, listed in full, 'pre-determined through a review of the most common nephrology subjects discussed in existing literature'; D2: the prompt for each chatbot is printed (three slightly different wordings), the run date is exact (1 August 2023) and the engines are named (ChatGPT GPT-3.5 as used, Bing Chat GPT-4.0, Bard PaLM2), but no exact version strings; D3: prompts 'differed slightly... as we modified the prompt to optimize their responses' per chatbot, so arms did not receive an identical prompt, and no settings or retry rules are reported; D4: verification used the provided DOI in PubMed first, then Google Scholar or Web of Science if not found or DOI incomplete/missing, with University of Hawaii library and Google search for books - a sequential multi-source check of five documented components (authors, title, journal, year/issue, DOI); D5: verification is not attributed to named individuals in Methods (author contributions list a validation role for five authors, who also include the investigators); D6: the paper never states that references were verified in duplicate or blinded, and no agreement figure is reported; D7: incomplete, fabricated, inaccurate and accurate are defined in Methods (fabricated = could not be found in the database; inaccurate = identified but at least one of five components incorrect) and counted apart for every chatbot (e.g. ChatGPT 76 accurate, 82 inaccurate, 32 fabricated, 9 incomplete); D8: all three chatbots and 12 topics are reported with duplicates and absent references counted, but the ChatGPT-4.0 arm was dropped - the stated reason is that it 'was unable to provide actual references but it solely provided examples of references despite our attempt to modify the prompt'.

D1: the same 12 nephrology topics, listed in full, selected as 'the critical aspects of nephrology' by the authors, with no external sampling frame; D2: the prompt is printed verbatim ('Please provide the references in Vancouver style and their links in recent literature on... name of the topic') and the model is versioned as ChatGPT-3.5 (03/23 Version), but no date on which the prompts were run is stated; D3: 'We selected all the results provided by ChatGPT', so no output selection, but the number of references requested per topic is not stated (610 emerged) and no settings are reported; D4: DOI was searched in PubMed first, then Google Scholar, with Web of Science used to cross-reference, and all six components (authors, title, journal, year, DOI, link) had to be correct for a reference to be authentic; D5: verification is described in the passive voice in Methods - author contributions list validation by S.S. and W.C., who were also investigators who ran the study; D6: the paper never states that verification was duplicated or blinded, and no agreement figure is reported; D7: fabricated (all elements forged/non-existent), incorrect (existing, at least one component inaccurate) and incomplete are defined in Methods and counted apart (378 existed, 192 fabricated, 40 incomplete, 122 authentic), with per-component error rates given (links 68%, DOI 54%); D8: all 12 topics are reported in Table 1, but the per-topic and overall figures are internally inconsistent - general nephrology is described as 62% authentic in the text while overall authenticity is 20%, and per-topic fabricated shares (1-18%) do not reconcile with the overall 31% fabricated rate.
